claim: Association with Lactiplantibacillus plantarum (Lp) improves the growth of larvae fed amino acid-imbalanced diets, even though Lp cannot produce the limiting amino acid.
source: Using chemically defined diets, we found that association with Lp improves the growth of larvae-fed amino acid-imbalanced diets, even though Lp cannot produce the limiting amino acid.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, which is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Lp supports host growth through a molecular dialogue that requires functional operons encoding ribosomal and transfer RNAs (r/tRNAs) in Lp.
source: We show that in this context Lp supports its host's growth through a molecular dialogue that requires functional operons encoding ribosomal and transfer RNAs (r/tRNAs) in Lp and the general control nonderepressible 2 (GCN2) kinase in Drosophila's enterocytes.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by genetic screen data in Figure 2 and developmental timing experiments.

claim: Lp supports host growth through a molecular dialogue that requires the general control nonderepressible 2 (GCN2) kinase in Drosophila's enterocytes.
source: We show that in this context Lp supports its host's growth through a molecular dialogue that requires functional operons encoding ribosomal and transfer RNAs (r/tRNAs) in Lp and the general control nonderepressible 2 (GCN2) kinase in Drosophila's enterocytes.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by GCN2 knockdown experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Lp's r/tRNAs are packaged in extracellular vesicles.
source: Our data indicate that Lp's r/tRNAs are packaged in extracellular vesicles and activate GCN2 in a subset of larval enterocytes, a mechanism necessary to remodel the intestinal transcriptome and ultimately to support anabolic growth.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by electron microscopy and RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Lp's r/tRNAs activate GCN2 in a subset of larval enterocytes.
source: Our data indicate that Lp's r/tRNAs are packaged in extracellular vesicles and activate GCN2 in a subset of larval enterocytes, a mechanism necessary to remodel the intestinal transcriptome and ultimately to support anabolic growth.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by microscopy data showing GCN2 activation in the anterior midgut (Figure 4) and the dependence on r/tRNA operons (Figure 5).

claim: GCN2 activation in enterocytes is necessary to remodel the intestinal transcriptome and support anabolic growth.
source: Our data indicate that Lp's r/tRNAs are packaged in extracellular vesicles and activate GCN2 in a subset of larval enterocytes, a mechanism necessary to remodel the intestinal transcriptome and ultimately to support anabolic growth.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by transcriptomic analysis (Figure 7) and developmental timing experiments with GCN2 knockdown (Figure 6).

claim: Drosophila melanogaster harbors simple bacterial communities, which individual components can be cultured aerobically.
source: Indeed, Drosophila harbours simple bacterial communities, which individual components can be cultured aerobically.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Drosophila as a model system.

claim: Drosophila can easily be bred axenically, allowing gnotobiotic studies.
source: Moreover, Drosophila can easily be bred axenically, allowing gnotobiotic studies.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Drosophila as a model system.

claim: Drosophila's main bacterial symbionts can be genetically engineered.
source: Finally, Drosophila's main bacterial symbionts can be genetically engineered, enabling deep mechanistical studies on both the host side and the microbe side.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Drosophila as a model system.

claim: Drosophila's symbiotic microbes modulate their host's post-embryonic growth.
source: In the past decade, Drosophila's symbiotic microbes were shown to modulate their host's post-embryonic growth (Shin et al., 2011; Storelli et al., 2011), reproduction (Elgart et al., 2016; Gould et al., 2018), lifespan (Keebaugh et al., 2019; Yamada et al., 2015), metabolism (Gnainsky et al., 2021; Kamareddine et al., 2018; Newell and Douglas, 2014), immunity (Iatsenko et al., 2018), social behaviour (Chen et al., 2019; Sharon et al., 2010), and food preference (Kim et al., 2021; Leitão-Gonçalves et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Drosophila's symbiotic microbes modulate their host's reproduction.
source: In the past decade, Drosophila's symbiotic microbes were shown to modulate their host's post-embryonic growth (Shin et al., 2011; Storelli et al., 2011), reproduction (Elgart et al., 2016; Gould et al., 2018), lifespan (Keebaugh et al., 2019; Yamada et al., 2015), metabolism (Gnainsky et al., 2021; Kamareddine et al., 2018; Newell and Douglas, 2014), immunity (Iatsenko et al., 2018), social behaviour (Chen et al., 2019; Sharon et al., 2010), and food preference (Kim et al., 2021; Leitão-Gonçalves et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Drosophila's symbiotic microbes modulate their host's lifespan.
source: In the past decade, Drosophila's symbiotic microbes were shown to modulate their host's post-embryonic growth (Shin et al., 2011; Storelli et al., 2011), reproduction (Elgart et al., 2016; Gould et al., 2018), lifespan (Keebaugh et al., 2019; Yamada et al., 2015), metabolism (Gnainsky et al., 2021; Kamareddine et al., 2018; Newell and Douglas, 2014), immunity (Iatsenko et al., 2018), social behaviour (Chen et al., 2019; Sharon et al., 2010), and food preference (Kim et al., 2021; Leitão-Gonçalves et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

source: In the past decade, Drosophila's symbiotic microbes were shown to modulate their host's post-embryonic growth (Shin et al., 2011; Storelli et al., 2011), reproduction (Elgart et al., 2016; Gould et al., 2018), lifespan (Keebaugh et al., 2019; Yamada et al., 2015), metabolism (Gnainsky et al., 2021; Kamareddine et al., 2018; Newell and Douglas, 2014), immunity (Iatsenko et al., 2018), social behaviour (Chen et al., 2019; Sharon et al., 2010), and food preference (Kim et al., 2021; Leitão-Gonçalves et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Drosophila's symbiotic microbes modulate their host's immunity.
source: In the past decade, Drosophila's symbiotic microbes were shown to modulate their host's post-embryonic growth (Shin et al., 2011; Storelli et al., 2011), reproduction (Elgart et al., 2016; Gould et al., 2018), lifespan (Keebaugh et al., 2019; Yamada et al., 2015), metabolism (Gnainsky et al., 2021; Kamareddine et al., 2018; Newell and Douglas, 2014), immunity (Iatsenko et al., 2018), social behaviour (Chen et al., 2019; Sharon et al., 2010), and food preference (Kim et al., 2021; Leitão-Gonçalves et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Drosophila's symbiotic microbes modulate their host's social behaviour.
source: In the past decade, Drosophila's symbiotic microbes were shown to modulate their host's post-embryonic growth (Shin et al., 2011; Storelli et al., 2011), reproduction (Elgart et al., 2016; Gould et al., 2018), lifespan (Keebaugh et al., 2019; Yamada et al., 2015), metabolism (Gnainsky et al., 2021; Kamareddine et al., 2018; Newell and Douglas, 2014), immunity (Iatsenko et al., 2018), social behaviour (Chen et al., 2019; Sharon et al., 2010), and food preference (Kim et al., 2021; Leitão-Gonçalves et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Drosophila's symbiotic microbes modulate their host's food preference.
source: In the past decade, Drosophila's symbiotic microbes were shown to modulate their host's post-embryonic growth (Shin et al., 2011; Storelli et al., 2011), reproduction (Elgart et al., 2016; Gould et al., 2018), lifespan (Keebaugh et al., 2019; Yamada et al., 2015), metabolism (Gnainsky et al., 2021; Kamareddine et al., 2018; Newell and Douglas, 2014), immunity (Iatsenko et al., 2018), social behaviour (Chen et al., 2019; Sharon et al., 2010), and food preference (Kim et al., 2021; Leitão-Gonçalves et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Amino acids produced by symbiotic bacteria can inhibit the production of the neuropeptide CNMamide in the gut, which represses preference for amino acids.
source: Symbiotic cues can be nutrients: for instance, amino acids (AA) produced by symbiotic bacteria can inhibit the production of the neuropeptide CNMamide in the gut, which represses preference for AA (Kim et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Sensing of symbiotic bacteria's cell wall components by gut cells leads to the production of digestive enzymes, which helps the larva digest dietary polypeptides and improves systemic growth.
source: Sensing of symbiotic bacteria's cell wall components by gut cells leads to the production of digestive enzymes, which helps the larva digest the dietary polypeptides and improves its systemic growth (Erkosar et al., 2015; Matos et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Acetate produced by symbiotic microbes alters the epigenome of enteroendocrine cells, which stimulates the secretion of the hormone tachykinin.
source: Acetate produced by symbiotic microbes alters the epigenome of enteroendocrine cells, which stimulates the secretion of the hormone tachykinin (Jugder et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Tachykinin promotes lipid utilisation in enterocytes.
source: Tachykinin then promotes lipid utilisation in nearby enterocytes (Kamareddine et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Drosophila larvae reach metamorphosis (pupariation) in 4–5 days in optimal nutritional conditions.
source: Drosophila's growth phase (larval stages) depends widely on the nutritional environment: larvae reach metamorphosis (pupariation) in 4–5 days in optimal nutritional conditions or up to 15–20 days in severe malnutrition conditions (Erkosar et al., 2013; Tennessen and Thummel, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Drosophila larvae reach metamorphosis (pupariation) in up to 15–20 days in severe malnutrition conditions.
source: Drosophila's growth phase (larval stages) depends widely on the nutritional environment: larvae reach metamorphosis (pupariation) in 4–5 days in optimal nutritional conditions or up to 15–20 days in severe malnutrition conditions (Erkosar et al., 2013; Tennessen and Thummel, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The main amino acid sensing pathways are the target-of-rapamycin (TOR) kinase pathway and the general control nonderepressible 2 (GCN2) kinase.
source: The main AA (or lack of) sensing pathways are the target-of-rapamycin (TOR) kinase pathway and the general control nonderepressible 2 (GCN2) kinase (Gallinetti et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: TOR and GCN2 kinases were first described in yeast.
source: Both kinases were first described in yeast (Dever et al., 1992; Heitman et al., 1991) and orthologous pathways were found in virtually all eukaryotes, including Drosophila (Olsen et al., 1998; Zhang et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Orthologous TOR and GCN2 pathways were found in virtually all eukaryotes, including Drosophila.
source: Both kinases were first described in yeast (Dever et al., 1992; Heitman et al., 1991) and orthologous pathways were found in virtually all eukaryotes, including Drosophila (Olsen et al., 1998; Zhang et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The TOR kinase forms two protein complexes: mTORC1 and mTORC2.
source: The TOR kinase forms two protein complexes: mTORC1 and mTORC2, which can be activated by many cues (Laplante and Sabatini, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: mTORC1 responds to high intracellular amino acid levels through the action of amino acid transporters and amino acid-binding cytosolic proteins.
source: Especially, mTORC1 responds to high intracellular AA levels through the action of AA transporters and AA-binding cytosolic proteins; conversely, AA scarcity represses TOR activity (Goberdhan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Amino acid scarcity represses TOR activity.
source: Especially, mTORC1 responds to high intracellular AA levels through the action of AA transporters and AA-binding cytosolic proteins; conversely, AA scarcity represses TOR activity (Goberdhan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: TOR increases translation through phosphorylation of 4E-BP and S6K.
source: Once activated, TOR increases translation through phosphorylation of 4E-BP and S6K (Ma and Blenis, 2009) and promotes systemic growth of Drosophila larvae (Colombani et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: TOR promotes systemic growth of Drosophila larvae.
source: Once activated, TOR increases translation through phosphorylation of 4E-BP and S6K (Ma and Blenis, 2009) and promotes systemic growth of Drosophila larvae (Colombani et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: GCN2 is activated by the quantity of uncharged tRNAs, a signature of hampered protein synthesis reflecting a scarcity in intracellular amino acids.
source: The best-characterized cue is the quantity of uncharged tRNAs, a signature of hampered protein synthesis reflecting a scarcity in intracellular AA (Masson, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Activation of GCN2 causes a global translational repression through phosphorylation of the eukaryotic initiation factor 2 (eIF2).
source: Activation of GCN2 causes a global translational repression through phosphorylation of the eukaryotic initiation factor 2 (eIF2) (Teske et al., 2011) except for a subset of mRNAs which translation is increased.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Upon GCN2 activation, translation of a subset of mRNAs is increased, including transcription factors such as ATF4 that promote adaptation to stress.
source: Activation of GCN2 causes a global translational repression through phosphorylation of the eukaryotic initiation factor 2 (eIF2) (Teske et al., 2011) except for a subset of mRNAs which translation is increased. Among these mRNAs, transcription factors such as ATF4 then promote adaptation to stress (Harding et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Ubiquitous knock-down of GCN2 in Drosophila larvae causes developmental delay.
source: Ubiquitous knock-down of GCN2 in Drosophila larvae causes developmental delay (Malzer et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Activation of GCN2 in dopaminergic neurons of the larval brain triggers a marked behavioural response leading to the avoidance of diets with an imbalanced amino acid composition.
source: Activation of GCN2 in dopaminergic neurons of the larval brain (Bjordal et al., 2014) or in the enterocytes of adult flies (Kim et al., 2021) trigger a marked behavioural response leading to the avoidance of diets with an imbalanced AA composition.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Activation of GCN2 in the enterocytes of adult flies triggers a marked behavioural response leading to the avoidance of diets with an imbalanced amino acid composition.
source: Activation of GCN2 in dopaminergic neurons of the larval brain (Bjordal et al., 2014) or in the enterocytes of adult flies (Kim et al., 2021) trigger a marked behavioural response leading to the avoidance of diets with an imbalanced AA composition.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: GCN2 in adult enterocytes regulates gut plasticity in response to amino acid/sugar imbalance.
source: In addition, GCN2 in adult enterocytes regulates gut plasticity in response to AA/sugar imbalance (Bonfini et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: GCN2 in the midgut or in the fat body is necessary for lifespan extension under dietary restriction.
source: Furthermore, GCN2 in the midgut or in the fat body is necessary for lifespan extension under dietary restriction (Kim et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: GCN2 in the fat body represses reproduction under amino acid scarcity.
source: Finally, GCN2 in the fat body represses reproduction under AA scarcity (Armstrong et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Undernutrition greatly delays the development of germ-free Drosophila larvae.
source: Although undernutrition greatly delays the development of germ-free (GF) Drosophila larvae (i.e. larvae lacking a microbiota), such delay can be buffered by the association of GF larvae with certain strains of symbiotic microbes (Gould et al., 2018; Keebaugh et al., 2018; Shin et al., 2011; Storelli et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The developmental delay of germ-free larvae under undernutrition can be buffered by the association with certain strains of symbiotic microbes.
source: Although undernutrition greatly delays the development of germ-free (GF) Drosophila larvae (i.e. larvae lacking a microbiota), such delay can be buffered by the association of GF larvae with certain strains of symbiotic microbes (Gould et al., 2018; Keebaugh et al., 2018; Shin et al., 2011; Storelli et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Growth promotion by symbiotic bacteria relies partly on nutrient provision.
source: Growth promotion relies partly on nutrient provision: for instance, the symbiotic bacterium Lactiplantibacillus plantarum (formerly named Lactobacillus plantarum [Zheng et al., 2020], hereinafter referred to as Lp) can provide certain AA, which allows the larva to grow in the absence of these specific AA (Consuegra et al., 2020b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Lactiplantibacillus plantarum can provide certain amino acids, which allows the larva to grow in the absence of these specific amino acids.
source: Growth promotion relies partly on nutrient provision: for instance, the symbiotic bacterium Lactiplantibacillus plantarum (formerly named Lactobacillus plantarum [Zheng et al., 2020], hereinafter referred to as Lp) can provide certain AA, which allows the larva to grow in the absence of these specific AA (Consuegra et al., 2020b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Decreasing the concentration of any essential amino acid by 70% caused growth delay in germ-free larvae.
source: As expected, decreasing the concentration of any EAA caused growth delay in GF larvae.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Decreasing the amount of Ile, Lys, Thr, Trp, or Val by 70% completely blocked the development of germ-free larvae, which stalled at the L2 or L3 stage.
source: Decreasing the amount of certain EAA (Ile, Lys, Thr, Trp, Val) completely blocked the development of GF larvae, which stalled at the L2 or L3 stage.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Decreasing the amount of Arg, His, Met, Leu, or Phe by 70% caused an important developmental delay in germ-free larvae compared to the FLY AA diet.
source: Decreasing the amount of the other EAA (Arg, His, Met, Leu, Phe) caused an important developmental delay in GF larvae compared to the FLY AA diet (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Association with Lp rescued the effects of limitation in any essential amino acid.
source: Association with Lp rescued the effects of limitation in any EAA (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: Lp's genome does not encode the enzymes necessary for the synthesis of branched-chained amino acids (leucine, isoleucine, and valine).
source: Lp's genome does not encode the enzymes necessary for the synthesis of branched-chained AA (BCAA: leucine, isoleucine, and valine) (Martino et al., 2016; Saguir and de Nadra, 2007; Teusink et al., 2005), and thus Lp cannot provide them to Drosophila (Consuegra et al., 2020b; Kim et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Lp cannot provide branched-chained amino acids to Drosophila.
source: Lp's genome does not encode the enzymes necessary for the synthesis of branched-chained AA (BCAA: leucine, isoleucine, and valine) (Martino et al., 2016; Saguir and de Nadra, 2007; Teusink et al., 2005), and thus Lp cannot provide them to Drosophila (Consuegra et al., 2020b; Kim et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Decreasing Val by 60% resulted in a strong delay in the growth of germ-free larvae, which was almost completely rescued by association with Lp.
source: Decreasing Val by 60% resulted in a strong delay in the growth of GF larvae, which was almost completely rescued by association with Lp (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Replacing the missing Val with an equal quantity of another essential amino acid (Leu or His) did not improve the development of germ-free larvae.
source: Replacing the missing Val with an equal quantity of another EAA (Leu or His) did not improve the development of GF larvae (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The developmental delay observed on imbalanced diet is due to amino acid imbalance rather than total amino acid scarcity.
source: This shows that the delay observed on imbalanced diet is due to AA imbalance rather than total AA scarcity.
evidence: This is inferred from the experiment showing that replacing missing Val with other amino acids did not improve development (Figure 1D).

claim: Further decreasing Val concentration (–80%, –90%) was lethal to germ-free larvae, but not to Lp-associated larvae.
source: Of note, further decreasing Val concentration (–80%, –90%) was lethal to GF larvae, but not to Lp-associated larvae (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Completely removing Val from the diet is lethal to both germ-free larvae and Lp-associated larvae.
source: Completely removing Val from the diet is lethal to both GF larvae and Lp-associated larvae as Lp is a Val auxotroph (Consuegra et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Increasing Val by 100% compared to its initial levels did not impact the development of germ-free or Lp-associated larvae.
source: On the contrary, increasing Val by 100% compared to its initial levels did not impact the development of GF or Lp-associated larvae (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Egg-to-pupa survival was not impacted by amino acid imbalance nor by association with Lp.
source: Moreover, egg-to-pupa survival was not impacted by AA imbalance nor by association with Lp (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Supplementing germ-free larvae with heat-killed Lp did not rescue the effects of an imbalanced diet on larval growth.
source: Finally, supplementing the GF larvae with heat-killed (HK) Lp did not rescue the effects of an imbalanced diet on larval growth, which shows that the Val brought by the inoculation of Lp at the beginning of the experiment is not sufficient to restore Val levels required for larval growth (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The Val brought by the inoculation of Lp at the beginning of the experiment is not sufficient to restore Val levels required for larval growth.
source: Finally, supplementing the GF larvae with heat-killed (HK) Lp did not rescue the effects of an imbalanced diet on larval growth, which shows that the Val brought by the inoculation of Lp at the beginning of the experiment is not sufficient to restore Val levels required for larval growth (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is inferred from the heat-killed Lp experiment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Lp association does not alter food intake on imbalanced or balanced diets.
source: We observed that Lp association does not alter food intake on imbalanced (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E) or balanced diets (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: On a yeast-based diet, Lp stimulates the expression of intestinal proteases in larvae, which improves amino acid absorption by increasing the release of amino acids from dietary polypeptide.
source: On a yeast-based diet, Lp stimulates the expression of intestinal proteases in larvae, which improves AA absorption by increasing the release of AA from dietary polypeptide (Erkosar et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Germ-free larvae fed an imbalanced diet (FLYAA –60% Val) showed a decrease in Val content in the hemolymph compared to germ-free larvae fed a balanced diet.
source: GF larvae fed an imbalanced diet (FLYAA –60% Val) showed a decrease in Val content in the hemolymph compared to GF larvae fed a balanced diet.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The decrease in Val content in the hemolymph of germ-free larvae fed an imbalanced diet was compensated upon association with Lp.
source: This decrease was compensated upon association with Lp (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Lp promotes physiological adaptation of its host to amino acid imbalance through increased amino acid absorption, which supports larval growth.
source: Therefore, we posit that Lp promotes physiological adaptation of its host to AA imbalance through increased AA absorption, which supports larval growth.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Lp increases Val levels in the hemolymph despite not producing Val.

claim: A genetic screen using a transposon insertion library of Lp identified 32 insertional mutants that resulted in delayed larval development on a severely imbalanced diet.
source: We applied a threshold of z-score >2.5 and identified 32 insertional mutants. Association with these mutants thus results in a delayed time of larval development on a severely imbalanced diet (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by genetic screen data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Nine candidates from the genetic screen resulted in a significant and robust developmental delay on an imbalanced diet upon association.
source: Thus, we discarded 23 false positives and retained only 9 candidates which resulted in a significant and robust developmental delay on an imbalanced diet upon association (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by validation experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Three candidates (B08.06, F09.11, and H04.06) showed growth defects on the diet and were not retained for further analysis.
source: Three candidates (B08.06, F09.11, and H04.06) showed growth defects on the diet and thus were not retained for further analysis.
evidence: This is supported by bacterial growth data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Six candidates (B12.11, C08.20, C09.09, D12.09, D12.16, F07.08) showed no growth defect and did not show any impairment at colonising the larval gut.
source: On the contrary, the remaining six candidates (B12.11, C08.20, C09.09, D12.09, D12.16, F07.08) showed no growth defect. Moreover, they did not show any impairment at colonising the larval gut (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by bacterial growth and colonization data shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: Four out of six selected candidates (mutants C09.09, D12.09, D12.16, and F07.08) showed independent transposon insertions in operons containing genes encoding tRNAs and/or rRNAs.
source: Interestingly, four out of the six candidates (mutants C09.09, D12.09, D12.16, and F07.08) showed independent transposon insertions in operons containing genes encoding tRNAs and/or rRNAs (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by genome sequencing data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The genome of Lp contains five operons encoding r/tRNAs.
source: The genome of Lp contains five operons encoding r/tRNAs.
evidence: This is stated as a fact based on genome analysis.

claim: C09.09 and F07.08 display independent insertions in the same operon, but at different loci.
source: C09.09 and F07.08 display independent insertions in the same operon, but at different loci (upstream the 16S rRNA for C09.09 and inside the 23S rRNA for F07.08, Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by genome sequencing data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Lp:Tnr/tRNA displays an ~3- to 4-fold reduction of 16S and 23S rRNA compared to Lp:Tncontrol.
source: We extracted total RNA from Lp cultured in liquid HD and found that despite the redundancy of r/tRNAs operon in Lp's genome Lp:Tnr/tRNA displays an ~3- to 4-fold reduction of 16S (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) and 23S (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) rRNA compared to Lp:Tncontrol, indicating that altering the sequence of a single r/tRNA operon is sufficient to compromise global rRNA levels in Lp cells without altering cell growth.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Altering the sequence of a single r/tRNA operon is sufficient to compromise global rRNA levels in Lp cells without altering cell growth.
source: We extracted total RNA from Lp cultured in liquid HD and found that despite the redundancy of r/tRNAs operon in Lp's genome Lp:Tnr/tRNA displays an ~3- to 4-fold reduction of 16S (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) and 23S (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) rRNA compared to Lp:Tncontrol, indicating that altering the sequence of a single r/tRNA operon is sufficient to compromise global rRNA levels in Lp cells without altering cell growth.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Lp:Tnr/tRNA shows reduced rRNA but normal growth.

claim: The deletion mutant LpΔopr/tRNA showed the same phenotype as the insertion mutants in terms of lack of rescue of amino acid imbalance.
source: The deletion mutant (hereinafter referred to as LpΔopr/tRNA) showed the same phenotype as the insertion mutants in terms of lack of rescue of AA imbalance (–60% Val, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C; –70% Leu, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), growth on imbalanced HD in the presence of larvae (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), larval gut colonisation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F), and reduction of the expression of the 16S (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G) and 23S (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H) rRNA (~3-fold reduction).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C-H.

claim: Lp produces extracellular vesicles of 70–200 nm in size.
source: We isolated extracellular vesicles from Lp's supernatant and imaged them using electron microscopy, revealing the presence of spherical structures of 70–200 nm of size (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In Lp cells, 16S rRNA and 23S rRNA are considerably more abundant than Thr-tRNA.
source: In cells, 16S rRNA and 23S rRNA were considerably more abundant than Thr-tRNA, as expected from previous studies (Giannoukos et al., 2012; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3B and citations to previous studies.

claim: In purified extracellular vesicles from Lp, there is an enrichment of Thr-tRNAs.
source: In purified vesicles, we observed an enrichment of Thr-tRNAs (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Most rRNA in purified extracellular vesicles were depleted by RNAse treatment, suggesting that they were contaminants from the supernatant.
source: Most rRNA were depleted by the RNAse treatment, suggesting that they were contaminants from the supernatant.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNAse treatment experiment shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Thr-tRNAs in purified extracellular vesicles were enriched after RNAse treatment.
source: On the contrary, Thr-tRNAs were enriched after RNAse treatment (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Lp's extracellular vesicles contain mostly tRNAs, which may allow their transfer to host cells.
source: These results suggest that Lp's extracellular vesicles contain mostly tRNAs, which may allow their transfer to host cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that tRNAs are enriched in vesicles and protected from RNAse.

claim: The GCN2 kinase can bind to and be activated by unloaded tRNAs.
source: The GCN2 kinase can bind to and be activated by unloaded tRNAs (Masson, 2019, p. 2) and rRNAs (Zhu and Wek, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The GCN2 kinase can bind to and be activated by rRNAs.
source: The GCN2 kinase can bind to and be activated by unloaded tRNAs (Masson, 2019, p. 2) and rRNAs (Zhu and Wek, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The GCN2 pathway is one of the main pathways that allow eukaryotic cells to adapt to amino acid imbalance.
source: Moreover, the GCN2 pathway is one of the main pathways that allow eukaryotic cells to adapt to AA imbalance (Gallinetti et al., 2013, p. 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: GCN2 is active in the gut of Drosophila.
source: Finally, GCN2 is active in the gut of Drosophila (Bonfini et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2021), where we observed Lp in close proximity to host's cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies and microscopy data.

claim: In Drosophila, the transcription factor ATF4 acts downstream of GCN2 and binds to recognition sites in the first intron of the gene 4E-BP to activate its transcription.
source: In Drosophila, the transcription factor ATF4 acts downstream of GCN2 and binds to recognition sites in the first intron of the gene 4E-BP (Thor in Drosophila) to activate its transcription (Kang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The 4E-BPintrondsRed reporter allows visualization of the pattern of activity of ATF4 downstream of GCN2 activation.
source: Kang and colleagues previously generated a transgenic line (4E-BPintrondsRed), which carries a fluorophore under the transcriptional control of the first intron of 4E-BP. This reporter thus allows to visualise the pattern of activity of ATF4 downstream of GCN2 activation (Kang et al., 2017; Vasudevan et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The 4E-BPintrondsRed reporter is expressed in the anterior midgut specifically in Lp-associated larvae, while this signal is absent from germ-free guts.
source: Conversely, the 4E-BPintrondsRed reporter was expressed in the anterior midgut specifically in Lp-associated larvae, while this signal was absent from GF guts (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, red squares, and Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and Figure 4A.

claim: Expression of the 4E-BPintrondsRed reporter in the anterior midgut depends on the association with Lp, but not on amino acid imbalance.
source: Interestingly, expression of the 4E-BPintrondsRed reporter in this region depends on the association with Lp, but not on AA imbalance as we observed it in larvae raised on either imbalanced diet (Figure 4A, top panel) or balanced diet (Figure 4A, bottom panel; quantification of the signal is shown in Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Lp can activate the 4E-BPintrondsRed reporter specifically in the anterior midgut, independently of dietary amino acid imbalance.
source: Lp can thus activate the 4E-BPintrondsRed reporter specifically in the anterior midgut, independently of dietary AA imbalance.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the reporter is activated in both balanced and imbalanced diets.

claim: Inhibition of GCN2 expression using tissue-specific in vivo RNAi completely abrogated the activation of the 4E-BPintrondsRed reporter by Lp in the anterior midgut of larvae reared on imbalanced diet.
source: Inhibition of GCN2 expression using tissue-specific in vivo RNAi (Dietzl et al., 2007) completely abrogated the activation of the 4E-BPintrondsRed reporter by Lp in the anterior midgut of larvae reared on imbalanced diet (Figure 4C and D) or balanced diet (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4C-F.

claim: Lp promotes GCN2 activity in the anterior midgut of larvae, independently of amino acid imbalance.
source: Therefore, our results establish that Lp promotes GCN2 activity in the anterior midgut of larvae, independently of AA imbalance.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Lp activates the GCN2 reporter in both balanced and imbalanced diets.

claim: On an imbalanced diet, LpΔopr/tRNA-associated larvae showed a reduced activation of GCN2 compared to WT-associated larvae.
source: On an imbalanced diet, LpΔopr/tRNA-associated larvae showed a reduced activation of GCN2 compared to WT-associated larvae, although this reduction did not reach statistical significance (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: On a balanced diet, GCN2 activation in LpΔopr/tRNA-associated larvae was comparable to GCN2 activation in germ-free larvae, and significantly reduced compared to GCN2 activation in Lp WT-associated larvae.
source: On a balanced diet, GCN2 activation in LpΔopr/tRNA-associated larvae was comparable to GCN2 activation in GF larvae, and significantly reduced compared to GCN2 activation in Lp WT-associated larvae (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: In short-term association on an imbalanced diet, activation of GCN2 was significantly reduced in Lp:Tnr/tRNA-associated larvae compared to Lp:Tncontrol-associated larvae.
source: In short-term association on an imbalanced diet, activation of GCN2 was significantly reduced in Lp:Tnr/tRNA-associated larvae compared to Lp:Tncontrol-associated larvae (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: At the highest dose tested (625 µg), bacterial tRNAs significantly increased the expression of the 4E-BPintrondsRed reporter in the anterior midgut.
source: At the highest dose tested (625 µg), bacterial tRNAs significantly increased the expression of the reporter in the anterior midgut (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: The effect of feeding bacterial tRNAs was comparable to the effect of feeding eukaryotic tRNAs, though slightly inferior.
source: This increase was comparable to the effect of feeding eukaryotic tRNAs to these larvae, though slightly inferior.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The effect of feeding tRNAs was minimal as compared to the association of larvae with Lp.
source: However, the effect was minimal as compared to the association of larvae with Lp (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Lp's tRNA may be direct activators of GCN2 in enterocytes.
source: These results therefore suggest that Lp's tRNA may be direct activators of GCN2 in enterocytes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that feeding bacterial tRNAs activates the GCN2 reporter.

claim: GCN2 knock-down in enterocytes caused a significant developmental delay in Lp-associated larvae compared to control larvae on an imbalanced diet.
source: On an imbalanced diet (–60% Val), GCN2 knock-down in enterocytes caused a significant developmental delay in Lp-associated larvae compared to control larvae (Figure 6A), a phenotype that we confirmed by using two other GCN2 RNAi lines (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B) and by measuring the efficacy of RNA interference against GCN2 expression in the midgut (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This is supported by developmental timing data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-D.

claim: GCN2 knock-down in enterocytes does not alter colonisation of the gut by Lp.
source: Of note, GCN2 knock-down in enterocytes does not alter colonisation of the gut by Lp (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by colonization data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: GCN2 is necessary for Lp to rescue the developmental delay due to Val limitation.
source: Taken together, our results indicate that GCN2 is necessary for Lp to rescue the developmental delay due to Val limitation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that GCN2 knockdown prevents Lp from rescuing the developmental delay.

claim: GCN2 is necessary for Lp to rescue development upon scarcity in Ile or Thr, but not in Trp or Lys.
source: We found that GCN2 is necessary for Lp to rescue development upon scarcity in Ile or Thr, but not in Trp or Lys (Figure 6C–F).
evidence: This is supported by developmental timing data shown in Figure 6C-F.

claim: GCN2 is necessary only when Lp cannot provide the limiting amino acid.
source: Lp can synthesise Lys and Trp, but not Ile (Consuegra et al., 2020b); therefore, it seems that GCN2 is necessary only when Lp cannot provide the limiting AA.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that GCN2 is required for rescue when Lp cannot synthesize the limiting amino acid.

claim: Control larvae reared on imbalanced diet in association with Lp:Tnr/tRNA showed a developmental delay compared to larvae associated with Lp:Tncontrol.
source: As expected, control larvae reared on imbalanced diet in association with Lp:Tnr/tRNA showed a developmental delay compared to larvae associated with Lp:Tncontrol (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is supported by developmental timing data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Larvae knocked-down for GCN2 in the enterocytes did not show a difference between association with Lp:Tnr/tRNA and association with Lp:Tncontrol.
source: On the contrary, larvae knocked-down for GCN2 in the enterocytes did not show a difference between association with Lp:Tnr/tRNA and association with Lp:Tncontrol (Figure 6I); in other words, the effect of the r/tRNA operon mutation was only observed when GCN2 is fully expressed.
evidence: This is supported by developmental timing data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: The effect of the r/tRNA operon mutation was only observed when GCN2 is fully expressed.
source: On the contrary, larvae knocked-down for GCN2 in the enterocytes did not show a difference between association with Lp:Tnr/tRNA and association with Lp:Tncontrol (Figure 6I); in other words, the effect of the r/tRNA operon mutation was only observed when GCN2 is fully expressed.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that GCN2 knockdown eliminates the difference between Lp:Tnr/tRNA and Lp:Tncontrol.

claim: There is a functional interaction between Lp's r/tRNAs and GCN2 in the larval gut.
source: This suggests a functional interaction between Lp's r/tRNAs and GCN2 in the larval gut and supports the notion that Lp's influence on host adaptation to AA imbalance relies on a molecular dialogue engaging symbiont r/tRNAs and the host GCN2 kinase.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic interaction experiments shown in Figure 6H and I.

claim: Acetobacter pomorum rescued the developmental delay due to amino acid imbalance to the same extent as Lp.
source: Ap rescued the developmental delay due to AA imbalance to the same extent as Lp (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by developmental timing data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Acetobacter pomorum's support to larval development upon Val limitation was independent of GCN2 expression in the gut.
source: However, conversely to Lp, Ap's support to larval development upon Val limitation was independent of GCN2 expression in the gut (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by developmental timing data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Acetobacter pomorum can produce Val and rescue the host's auxotrophy to Val.
source: This is likely explained by the ability of Ap to produce Val and rescue the host's auxotrophy to Val (Consuegra et al., 2020b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Acetobacter pomorum did not activate GCN2 in the anterior midgut of larvae on imbalanced diet or balanced diet.
source: Interestingly, Ap did not activate GCN2 in the anterior midgut of larvae on imbalanced diet (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C and D) or balanced diet (Figure 6—figure supplement 2E and F).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C-F.

claim: The ability to activate GCN2 in the anterior midgut is not common to all symbiotic bacteria and a specific attribute of Lp-mediated benefit.
source: Therefore, the ability to activate GCN2 in the anterior midgut is not common to all symbiotic bacteria and a specific attribute of Lp-mediated benefit.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Ap does not activate GCN2 while Lp does.

claim: GCN2 knock-down in the fat body had no impact on the development of Lp-associated larvae fed an imbalanced diet.
source: We used the driver C564-Gal4 to knock down GCN2 expression in the fat body as well as other tissues such as salivary glands and hemocytes (Takehana et al., 2004). This had no impact on the development of Lp-associated larvae fed an imbalanced diet (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F), which suggests that the phenotype that we observed engages GCN2 in enterocytes rather than in other tissues.
evidence: This is supported by developmental timing data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The TOR pathway was not required in the fat body or in enterocytes for Lp to rescue amino acid imbalance.
source: Of note, although the TOR pathway is another major factor supporting systemic host growth in the fat body (Colombani et al., 2003) and in enterocytes (Redhai et al., 2020), it was not required in the fat body (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G) nor in enterocytes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1H) for Lp to rescue AA imbalance.
evidence: This is supported by developmental timing data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G and H.

claim: The TOR pathway was important to support the growth of germ-free animals.
source: However, it was important to support the growth of GF animals (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G and H).
evidence: This is supported by developmental timing data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G and H.

claim: Knocking down ATF4 or 4E-BP in the enterocytes delayed the development of germ-free larvae on an imbalanced diet.
source: We observed that knocking down ATF4 or 4E-BP in the enterocytes delayed the development of GF larvae on an imbalanced diet.
evidence: This is supported by developmental timing data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: ATF4 and 4E-BP knock-downs did not affect the development of Lp-associated larvae like GCN2 knock-down did.
source: However, such knock-downs did not affect the development of Lp-associated larvae like GCN2 knock-down did.
evidence: This is supported by developmental timing data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: ATF4 and 4E-BP are not required for Lp to support larval development upon dietary amino acid imbalance.
source: ATF4 and 4E-BP are thus not required for Lp to support larval development upon dietary AA imbalance (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ATF4 and 4E-BP knockdowns do not prevent Lp from rescuing the developmental delay.

claim: The GCN2 pathway in enterocytes mediates Lp's support to larval development despite dietary amino acid imbalance, independently of TOR and ATF4.
source: Taken together, our results demonstrate a specific role of the GCN2 pathway in enterocytes to mediate Lp's support to larval development despite dietary AA imbalance, independently of TOR and ATF4.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined results of GCN2, TOR, and ATF4 knockdown experiments.

claim: 104 genes were consistently differentially expressed by Lp in a GCN2-dependent, ATF4-independent, and r/tRNA operon-dependent manner (25 up-regulated and 79 down-regulated).
source: We applied the four aforementioned selective filters (Figure 7A) to our dataset and found 104 genes consistently DE (25 up-regulated and 79 down-regulated) by Lp in a GCN2-dependent, ATF4-independent, and r/tRNA operon-dependent manner (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: This is supported by transcriptomic analysis shown in Figure 7B and C.

claim: Gene Ontology enrichment analysis of down-regulated genes showed significant enrichment in GO terms associated with mitochondrial respiration, resistance to oxidative stress and negative regulation of cell proliferation.
source: We found a significant enrichment in GO terms associated with mitochondrial respiration, resistance to oxidative stress and negative regulation of cell proliferation (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by Gene Ontology enrichment analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The decrease in genes responsible for mitochondrial respiration in the anterior midgut of Lp-associated larvae suggests that the organ is undergoing remodelling and proliferation.
source: Therefore, the decrease in genes responsible for mitochondrial respiration that we observe in the anterior midgut of Lp-associated larvae suggests that the organ is ongoing remodelling and proliferation.
evidence: This is inferred from the transcriptomic data and knowledge about metabolic shifts during proliferation.

claim: Gene Ontology enrichment analysis of up-regulated genes showed significant enrichment for GO terms associated with organ morphogenesis, cell differentiation, and cell proliferation.
source: We detected a significant enrichment for GO terms associated with organ morphogenesis, cell differentiation (different cell types: neurons or epithelial cells), and cell proliferation (especially members of the epidermal growth factor receptor [EGFR] pathway) (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by Gene Ontology enrichment analysis shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Lp enhances the growth and maturation of the anterior midgut in a GCN2-dependent, ATF4-independent, and r/tRNA operon-dependent manner.
source: These signatures suggest that Lp enhances the growth and maturation of the anterior midgut in a GCN2-dependent, ATF4-independent, and r/tRNA operon-dependent manner.
evidence: This is inferred from the transcriptomic signatures shown in Figure 7.

claim: The transcriptomic analysis identified GCN2-dependent, ATF4-independent, and Lp r/tRNA operon-dependent signatures evoking increased epithelium maturation and altered metabolic activity which would together support tissue growth and maturation.
source: Taken together, our transcriptomic analysis of the anterior midgut of larvae growing in an imbalanced diet allowed us to identify GCN2-dependent, ATF4-independent, and Lp r/tRNA operon-dependent signatures evoking increased epithelium maturation and altered metabolic activity which would together support tissue growth and maturation.
evidence: This is inferred from the transcriptomic analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: fezzik was among the top genes whose expression was repressed by Lp in a GCN2-dependent, ATF4-independent, r/tRNA operon-dependent manner.
source: We noted that fezzik (fiz) was among the top genes whose expression was repressed by Lp in a GCN2-dependent, ATF4-independent, r/tRNA operon-dependent manner (Figure 7F and Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by transcriptomic data shown in Figure 7F and Figure 8A.

claim: fezzik is predicted to be an oxidoreductase.
source: fezzik is predicted to be an oxidoreductase (Iida et al., 2007), possibly involved in ecdysone metabolism (McQuilton et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Larvae carrying an hypomorphic allele of fezzik or ubiquitously knocked down for fezzik display accelerated development.
source: Importantly, larvae carrying an hypomorphic allele of fezzik or ubiquitously knocked down for fezzik display accelerated development (Glaser-Schmitt and Parsch, 2018), which suggests that fezzik is a systemic growth repressor.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: fezzik is a systemic growth repressor.
source: Importantly, larvae carrying an hypomorphic allele of fezzik or ubiquitously knocked down for fezzik display accelerated development (Glaser-Schmitt and Parsch, 2018), which suggests that fezzik is a systemic growth repressor.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that fezzik loss-of-function accelerates development.

claim: fezzik knock-down in enterocytes accelerated the development of germ-free larvae, Lp-associated larvae, and LpΔopr/tRNA-associated larvae.
source: fezzik knock-down in enterocytes accelerated the development of GF larvae, Lp-associated larvae, and LpΔopr/tRNA-associated larvae (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by developmental timing data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: fezzik inhibition through GCN2 activation and r/tRNAs contributes to the rescue of developmental delay by Lp on imbalanced diet.
source: These results suggest that fezzik inhibition through GCN2 activation and r/tRNAs contributes to the rescue of developmental delay by Lp on imbalanced diet.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that fezzik knockdown accelerates development in all conditions.

claim: GCN2 may have evolved as a sensor of symbiotic cues, allowing the larva to couple its growth with the abundance of microbes present in the environment.
source: GCN2 may have evolved as a sensor of symbiotic cues, allowing the larva to couple its growth with the abundance of microbes present in the environment: when microbes are abundant, symbiotic cues may activate GCN2 in the gut, triggering gut growth, optimal nutrient absorption, and rapid organismal growth.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: GCN2 is highly conserved across eukaryotes.
source: GCN2 is highly conserved across eukaryotes (Donnelly et al., 2013), and is important for mouse adaptation to an AA-imbalanced diet (Anthony et al., 2004; Guo and Cavener, 2007; Laeger et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2002, p. 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: GCN2 is important for mouse adaptation to an amino acid-imbalanced diet.
source: GCN2 is highly conserved across eukaryotes (Donnelly et al., 2013), and is important for mouse adaptation to an AA-imbalanced diet (Anthony et al., 2004; Guo and Cavener, 2007; Laeger et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2002, p. 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.
